source.title: Mapping the Existing Return-to-Sport Criteria After Pectoralis Major Tendon Injury in Different Sports: A Scoping Review for Getting Back to the Game

paper.citation: Sharma S., Whiteley R., Rani B., Sartori S., Sharma H., Gabbett T.J. Mapping the Existing Return-to-Sport Criteria After Pectoralis Major Tendon Injury in Different Sports: A Scoping Review for Getting Back to the Game. Sports Health: A Multidisciplinary Approach. 2026;18(3):685-696. doi:10.1177/19417381251408058.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which criteria have been used to clear adult athletes for return to sport after surgical or nonsurgical management of complete or incomplete pectoralis major tendon injury? Participants: 1,129 injured athletes across 39 studies; only one participant was female and the reported mean age was 30.1 years. Sport and level: Elite and recreational contact and noncontact sport, including NFL football, rugby, wrestling, weightlifting, and bench press. Design: OSF-registered PRISMA-ScR scoping review. Exposure or intervention: Surgical and conservative management with any rehabilitation approach.
paper.tldr: Thirty-nine studies were included: 33 case reports/series, five cohort/longitudinal studies, and one epidemiological study. The evidence represented 1,129 athletes but only one female; 841 athletes returned to sport among studies reporting the outcome, while 216 were reported to return fully to preinjury performance. There is no evidence-supported single test or timeline for pectoralis-major clearance.
paper.methods: Design: OSF-registered PRISMA-ScR scoping review. Exposure or intervention: Surgical and conservative management with any rehabilitation approach. Comparator: No required comparator; designs included case reports/series, cohorts, and epidemiology. Measurements and outcomes: Rehabilitation protocol, strength, range of motion, pain, functional outcomes, return time/rate, return to preinjury performance, and reinjury. Analysis: Multi-database and grey-literature search, blinded independent screening, consensus resolution, and descriptive evidence mapping.
paper.findings: Thirty-nine studies were included: 33 case reports/series, five cohort/longitudinal studies, and one epidemiological study. The evidence represented 1,129 athletes but only one female; 841 athletes returned to sport among studies reporting the outcome, while 216 were reported to return fully to preinjury performance. Surgery was the primary management in 38 of 39 studies, and no included study reported a specific standardized rehabilitation protocol. Mean reported return-to-sport time was 7.5 months across 30 studies, with substantial variation from three months to four years. No included study reported specific, objective, validated clearance criteria; commonly measured domains were strength, range of motion, pain, and functional scales. Return to sport/participation was reported in 34 of 39 studies, but return to preinjury performance was reported in only 20 of 39.
paper.limitations: The evidence base was dominated by case reports and series, limiting causal and prognostic inference. Almost all participants were male, so applicability to female athletes is unknown. The review mapped criteria but did not test their predictive validity for successful or durable return. Management approaches, injury location/severity, sports, athlete levels, rehabilitation, and outcome definitions were heterogeneous. The review could not determine how treatment choice affected return-to-sport or return-to-performance success across sports. A mean return time is descriptive, not a clearance criterion, and should not be interpreted as a safe universal threshold.
paper.practicalImplications: There is no evidence-supported single test or timeline for pectoralis-major clearance. A multidisciplinary decision should document tissue healing and symptoms, active range of motion, bilateral adduction/flexion/rotation strength and endurance, kinetic-chain function, psychological readiness, progressive contact and sport-specific loading, and the athlete's positional demands and risk tolerance. Returning to participation, returning to sport, and returning to prior performance should be tracked separately.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, there is no evidence-supported single test or timeline for pectoralis-major clearance. A multidisciplinary decision should document tissue healing and symptoms, active range of motion, bilateral adduction/flexion/rotation strength and endurance, kinetic-chain function, psychological readiness, progressive contact and sport-specific loading, and the athlete's positional demands and risk tolerance. Returning to participation, returning to sport, and returning to prior performance should be tracked separately. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, there is no evidence-supported single test or timeline for pectoralis-major clearance. A multidisciplinary decision should document tissue healing and symptoms, active range of motion, bilateral adduction/flexion/rotation strength and endurance, kinetic-chain function, psychological readiness, progressive contact and sport-specific loading, and the athlete's positional demands and risk tolerance. Returning to participation, returning to sport, and returning to prior performance should be tracked separately. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
